base_override.reason: The engine's conservative OE (OCF − capex − SBC) is not a usable base for a broker-dealer: OCF carries balance-sheet plumbing — advisor-loan book growth and client receivable/payable swings — not distributable cash (NI_OCF_DIVERGENCE fires for 2023, 2024 and 2025; FY2025 OCF was −$411M against net income of +$863M, and ttm.py's TTM conservative OE is also negative at −$12.68/share). The result is a mechanical Tier F for a company with positive net income in every year of the 10-year history. The engine's maintenance definition — the same net-income-based treatment this sweep applied to IBKR — is the defensible owner's-earnings proxy for this sector; the median-of-3-FY normalization mirrors the engine's own base method applied to that definition. Declared under bounded authority (c): every input is a figure printed by this run's engine output.
base_override.source: Median of the last 3 fiscal years' maintenance owner's earnings per share, built exclusively from this run's financials_history.csv (the engine's own oe_maintenance column: net income + D&A − min(capex, D&A) − change in net working capital ex cash/debt): FY2023 oe_maintenance $1,066,250,000 / 77,861,000 diluted shares = $13.6943; FY2024 $1,058,616,000 / 75,427,000 = $14.0350; FY2025 $863,024,000 / 79,061,000 = $10.9159; median of the three = $13.6943.

moat_against: Advisors are independent contractors who own the client relationship — the asset base can walk; Commonwealth teams have already defected to Cetera
Scaled, credible rivals on both sides: Schwab/Fidelity custody economics and Cetera/Osaic/Raymond James competing for the same advisors
Earnings geared to exogenous variables: equity-market levels drive asset-based fees; Fed cuts compress client cash-sweep economics (Q2 2026 net interest income fell sharply YoY)
Growth is increasingly bought, not built: Commonwealth ($2.7B) and Atria were debt-funded, and retention (~90% targeted) is not yet proven through the Q4 2026 onboarding
moat_for: Largest US independent advisor platform — ~32,000 advisors, $2.56T client assets (Q2 2026); scale in tech/compliance/custody small rivals cannot match
Advisor switching costs are real: moving a practice means repapering every client account and changing custodian/clearing
Recruiting flywheel: $89B recruited assets TTM, $23.1B organic net new assets in Q2 2026 alone (4.0% annualized)
Recurring revenue mix: advisory assets 60.4% of client assets and rising; multiple affiliation models widen the funnel
moat_justification: Largest independent broker-dealer platform in the US (~32,000 advisors, $2.56T client assets at Q2 2026): scale in technology, compliance, custody and clearing that a small firm cannot replicate, real advisor switching costs (moving a practice means repapering every client account), a recruiting flywheel (TTM recruited assets $89B) and recurring advisory fees (60.4% of client assets) — against the structural weakness that advisors are independent contractors who own the client relationship and can walk (Commonwealth teams have already left for Cetera), credible scaled rivals (Schwab, Fidelity, Raymond James, Cetera, Osaic), and earnings geared to equity-market levels (asset-based fees) and policy rates (client cash sweep).
name: LPL Financial Holdings Inc.
one_liner: Quality advisor-platform compounder, moat 6/10 — the engine's mechanical Tier F is a sector artifact (broker-dealer OCF is advisor-loan and client-balance plumbing, not cash earnings); on the corrected maintenance-earnings base of $13.69/share the $323.46 price yields a 9.9% weighted IRR with IV@15% of $180.50, so it clears the 15% hurdle only below ~$181 (~$144 with a margin of safety).
